style.summary:
style of A: A speaks in clipped, unfinished fragments and keeps a cooperative, exploratory tone.
style of B: B speaks assertively, repeatedly restates the point with 'what I'm arguing', and interrupts with a firm, contrastive delivery.

A: A's cooperative tone invites B to build on A's idea rather than contest it, which gives A a constructive lead.
A's opening remark 'this is why we started to look' presents A's motivation as the reason the discussion exists.
A's clipped fragments are left for B to finish, which places the completion of A's thought in B's hands.
B: B interrupts A twice and keeps the floor, which projects control over how the exchange unfolds.
B repeats 'what I'm arguing' to keep the agenda on B's position, which signals a firm commitment to the claim.
B's contrastive framing of the phonemes as idealised, against 'reality', casts B as the speaker who sees the problem clearly.

A: A's cooperative tone reads as yielding to B's interruptions, so it reflects B's control of the turn rather than A's leadership.
A's opening motivation is a premise that B immediately contests, so the framing does not hold for A once B takes it up.
A's unfinished fragments show A being cut off, and B's completion of them is B taking over the thought.
B: B's interruptions come with stutters and restarts, which suggests B struggling to get a sentence out rather than commanding the floor.
Repeating 'what I'm arguing' signals that B still needs to persuade A, so A's acceptance of the point is what remains open.
B's contrastive framing still rests on A's premise about phonemes, so the substance of the disagreement is A's to define.

content.summary:
content of A: A introduces the idea of voiced phonemes as a starting point for the approach.
content of B: B challenges that starting point by pointing to the overlap and variability found in actual speech.

A: A's introduction of voiced phonemes sets the concept that the rest of the discussion is organised around.
A's account of why the team started with phonemes gives A the historical framing of the work.
A's naming of the concept forces B to respond to A's terms.
B: B's point about overlap in real speech supplies the key empirical fact that challenges the simplified model.
B's claim that the phoneme intuition is misleading shifts the substance of the conversation to B's account.
B's contrast between the idealised picture and actual speech positions B as the one describing reality.

A: A's starting concept is directly contested by B, so the framing of the discussion is moved away from A's terms.
A's account of motivation is incomplete and B's challenge determines what the discussion is about.
A's naming of the concept is only the topic, and B's response decides what the concept is taken to mean.
B: B's overlap point is presented as a qualification of the simpler model, so the empirical claim depends on A's framing.
B's claim about the intuition is still addressed to A's proposal, so the conversation remains organised around A's idea.
B's description of reality is stated without evidence in the excerpt, so it is an assertion rather than a settled fact.

coordination.summary:
coordination of A: A starts sentences that are cut off, so the turns are repeatedly handed to B.
coordination of B: B takes the floor at each opening, completes the turns of A, and returns to the main argument.

A: A opens the topic and starts the turns, which gives A the first move in each exchange.
A's cooperative pauses make room for B to speak, so A keeps the exchange open for discussion.
A returns to the phonemes after B's interruption, which keeps the topic tied to A's proposal.
B: B interrupts A twice in quick succession, which claims the floor at the moments that matter.
B's repeated 'what I'm arguing' keeps the turn order tied to B's line of reasoning.
B takes the longer turn that carries the main counterpoint about reality.

A: A's openings are cut off each time, which means A does not keep the floor long enough to shape the turn order.
Pauses that make room for B are a concession rather than a sign that A sets the pace, so B decides when to speak.
A's return to the phonemes is a response to B's pressure, so the thread is following B's challenge.
B: B's interruptions are stuttered restarts, which show B struggling to hold the floor rather than controlling it.
B's repeated framing shows B still arguing for a point A has not accepted, so the turn order is not settled by B.
B's longer turn is a reply to A's opening, so the length follows A's cue rather than B's control.

engagement.summary:
engagement of A: A returns to the phonemes and explains the origin of the approach, which shows interest in the idea.
engagement of B: B presses the argument with repeated restatements and an engaged account of overlap, which shows strong investment.

A: A explains the motivation behind the work, which shows personal investment in the approach.
A's cooperative tone signals openness to B's view, which keeps A engaged with the other speaker.
A's return to the phonemes shows A is attached to the idea and willing to defend it.
B: B's repeated 'what I'm arguing' shows a strong investment in convincing A of the point.
B's engagement with overlap and variability shows close attention to the real problem.
B's interruptions show eagerness to take part in the argument.

A: A's motivation is stated as background and does not show that A is invested in the outcome of the disagreement.
Cooperative tone can be a way of avoiding conflict, so it does not show that A is actively engaged in the argument.
Returning to the phonemes may be a reaction to B's challenge rather than a sign of A's investment in defending it.
B: B's restatements show frustration with A's position, which signals more pressure than engagement.
B's point about overlap is presented as a limitation of the model, so it is a critique rather than shared investment.
Interrupting is a habit of taking the floor, and it does not show that B is more invested in the topic than A.
